extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and political theory; anyone studying Plato's Republic or the nature/education of rulers
extracted.subtask_description: A Socratic dialogue section specifying the character, education, selection, and civic role of true philosophers and guardians — why philosophers are undervalued, how they may be corrupted, and what training and tests are required for them to rule well.

rubrics_metrics.name: True philosopher’s nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lover of knowledge always striving after being; will not rest in the multiplicity of individuals but seeks the knowledge of the true nature of every essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He follows truth as his leader, draws near to true being, 'having begotten mind and truth, he will have knowledge and will live and grow truly,' and will 'not rest in the multiplicity of individuals which is an appearance only.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher hates falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosopher’s nature excludes love of lies; he will 'utterly hate a lie.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When truth is the captain, the band he leads gives no cause for suspicion: 'Justice and health of mind will be of the company, and temperance will follow after.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent virtues of the philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosopher has natural gifts such as courage, magnificence, apprehension, memory, temperance and similar qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues are listed as the philosopher’s natural endowments, but each may interact with education/environment to support or distract from philosophical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy is dangerous to greatness when pursued wrongly
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the philosopher’s virtues and ordinary goods (beauty, wealth, strength, rank, connections) can 'destroy and distract from philosophy' the soul which possesses them when conditions are alien.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finest natures are more sensitive to poor nurture; 'the most gifted minds, when they are ill-educated, become pre-eminently bad.' Education and environment must be appropriate to preserve rare natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion corrupts and displaces true education
rubrics_metrics.description: The many (public assemblies, courts, theatres, camps) teach the opinion of the many and thereby shape young people to the tastes of the mob rather than to true virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public praise and blame, clapping, and the 'echo of the rocks' overwhelm private training; the 'new Sophists and educators' also use coercion (attainder, confiscation, death) when speech fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophists as mercenary teachers of popular opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Those called Sophists teach nothing but the opinions and tempers of the many; they learn to please the beast (the many) and call that wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They produce rules of honour and shame based on popular taste, not on understanding principles; their output are 'sophisms captivating to the ear, having nothing in them genuine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers will be despised by a mutinous populace
rubrics_metrics.description: In states ruled by the 'mutinous sailors' (those who seize authority), the true helmsman (philosopher) will be called a prater, star-gazer, or good-for-nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy to the pilot shows that competence and technical art are not rewarded when a crew is in mutiny; philosophers are similarly undervalued when society does not accept their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper relation of ruler and art (no begging for obedience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pilot (ruler) should not humbly beg sailors to be commanded; those who need governing should seek the one able to govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The natural order is that the qualified rule; rulers should not have to solicit obedience—competence should command respect, just as a physician is sought by the sick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by tested patriotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be lovers of the country and tested by pleasures and pains so as not to lose patriotism in hardships or dangers; those who fail are rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selection test is moral and practical: the candidate must 'always come forth pure, like gold tried in the refiner’s fire' and merit honours in life and after death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity and composite nature of ideal guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: The full set of gifts required for guardians—quick intelligence, memory, sagacity, high-spiritedness, magnanimity, steadiness in battle, and capacity for intellectual toil—rarely occur together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these qualities are often found only 'in shreds and patches', the class of perfect guardians will be small; education must try to cultivate multiple faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous, staged education for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should follow a life-stage curriculum: childhood/youth studies suited to tender years, bodily gymnastics early, increasing 'gymnastics of the soul' as intellect matures, and later freedom to engage in philosophy when civil/military strength declines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to present practice (where youth dabble and then leave philosophy), the guardians 'must take the longer circuit, and toil at learning as well as at gymnastics' so they 'may reach the highest knowledge of all.'

rubrics_metrics.name: End goal: knowledge of the good (highest knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest knowledge toward which the guardians must be trained is the idea of the good, which makes other things useful and advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue treats the idea of the good as the summit of education: nothing short of the most finished picture should satisfy; 'we know so little' but it remains the proper calling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth before depth — probation across many knowledges
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate must be exercised in many kinds of knowledge to see whether the soul can endure the highest studies or will faint under them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing must include a wide curriculum to reveal endurance and aptitude for advanced dialectic; guardians must be tried beyond merely military or bodily tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding seductive imitators of philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Unworthy persons who enter philosophy (like 'bald little tinkers' newly enriched) produce bastard marriages with philosophy, generating sophisms and corrupt forms that dishonour the pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These imitators are attracted by showy titles and 'a land well stocked with fair names'; their presence causes public reprobation of philosophy because they are incompetent and deceitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of philosopher by suitable polity
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy flourishes only in a State fitted to it; in degenerate governments the philosophic nature is 'warped and estranged' and the philosopher becomes denaturalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a State matches the perfection of philosophy, then the philosopher will be divine in effect; otherwise the best natures are corrupted by the human institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgiver as imitator of divine pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who fashion constitutions must first erase the existing picture and trace from absolute justice/beauty/temperance an outline, mixing elements until the human copy resembles the divine pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislator should 'rub out the picture, and leave a clean surface' and only then inscribe laws after looking 'upwards and downwards' to ideal forms; the process is hard but necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-rulers should be compelled by necessity or divine inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Either philosophers must be compelled by superior power to take charge of the State, or rulers (kings, princes) must be divinely inspired to love true philosophy; without such necessity, the arrangement is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges difficulty but denies impossibility: if such compulsion or divine selection occurs, the ideal polity becomes realizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers must not occupy philosophy as a side-business
rubrics_metrics.description: Students of philosophy should not treat it as a pastime or only as time 'saved from moneymaking and housekeeping' — they must devote sustained life-long study, not intermittent attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current practice leads to extinguishing the philosophic spirit; instead, the life of a guardian-philosopher requires continuous, progressive engagement culminating in dialectic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral aim: imitate the divine order
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'holds converse with the divine order' and thereby becomes 'orderly and divine' as far as human nature allows, imitating fixed and immutable things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This moral orientation explains why philosophers avoid malice and envy and why their focus is on things stable rather than transient human affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical analogy: technical expertise of the helmsman
rubrics_metrics.description: The true pilot must pay attention to year, seasons, sky, stars, and winds and be the steerer; this is an analogy for the philosopher's art required for the command of a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just as a pilot must master his craft to be fit for command, so must the ruler-philosopher master knowledge and art of governance; otherwise mutinous elements will deride him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation or private retreat when governance is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some philosophers, seeing that they cannot be effective in corrupt States and unable singly to resist wickedness, choose to 'hold his peace, and go his own way,' preserving personal purity rather than risking futile sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such retreat is commended as doing 'a great work' if a State suitable to him cannot be found; nevertheless greater good would be achieved if a suitable State existed.
